instruction: Why are some months longer than others?
reference: That is a great calendar question! The length of our months comes from a mix of history and astronomy. The ancient Romans based their calendar on the Moon's phases, but because the Moon takes about 29.5 days to orbit Earth, keeping a twelve-month calendar aligned with Earth's 365.25-day trip around the Sun required some adjustments. Julius Caesar and later Emperor Augustus added days to different months to make the math work out. February ended up with the leftover days, which is why it is the shortest, while the others got 30 or 31 days to make sure the whole year matches the solar cycle.
prediction: Months get their lengths from the Earth's orbit around the Sun, which isn't a perfect circle but an ellipse. As we travel around the Sun, the Earth is tilted on its axis, and different parts of the planet receive more or less direct sunlight at different times. This means that some months see more daylight and warmer temperatures, while others have cooler nights and shorter days. To account for these variations, the ancient Romans divided the year into twelve months, giving us the current system where February has fewer days because it was originally added to keep the calendar in sync with the seasons over thousands of years.

instruction: Why do we celebrate New Year's on January 1st?
reference: We celebrate New Year's on January 1st because of the calendar system we use, called the Gregorian calendar. This tradition goes back to ancient Rome in 45 BCE, when Julius Caesar introduced the Julian calendar and dedicated January 1st to Janus, the Roman god of beginnings, gates, and transitions. Later, in 1582, Pope Gregory XIII refined it into the calendar we use today, keeping January 1st as the official start of the new year to mark a fresh beginning.
prediction: We celebrate New Year's Day on January 1st because it was originally set as the beginning of the Roman calendar, which was based on the cycles of the moon rather than the sun. The Romans wanted to mark the start of a fresh new year, and they chose January 1st because it was the first day of the month. Over time, the Gregorian calendar, which is used in most countries today, shifted the date forward by eleven days due to a mistake in calculating leap years. That's why 1900 wasn't a leap year, but 2000 was!

instruction: What makes ice float?
reference: Ice floats because water actually expands when it freezes! Most substances become denser when they turn from liquid to solid, but water molecules form a special crystal structure when they freeze into ice, which spaces them further apart. Because of this, ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats right to the top.
prediction: Ice floats because it is less dense than water! Water molecules form hydrogen bonds in a hexagonal structure, which creates a rigid lattice. When water freezes into ice, the molecules slow down and pack closer together into a crystalline structure, making the overall density lower. This unique property of ice is why you can stack ice cubes on top of each other without them sinking.

instruction: How does food become spicy?
reference: Food gets its spicy kick from a special chemical compound called capsaicin! Plants like chili peppers actually make capsaicin as a natural defense mechanism to stop animals and bugs from eating them. When you eat something spicy, the capsaicin tricks the pain receptors on your tongue into thinking your mouth is actually getting hot, which is why it feels like a fire!

When you eat them, the capsaicinoids interact with special pain sensors in your tongue and nose called TRPV1 receptors. These receptors send signals to your brain that make it feel like the heat is spreading all over your mouth, giving you that fiery sensation.

instruction: Why do some people have allergies?

That overreaction is what causes symptoms like sneezing, itchy eyes, or a runny nose!

Some people inherit genes that make their immune systems more sensitive, while others might be exposed to allergens early in life.
